chapter: Long Island years and Battle's estate
title: ASCAP royalties and checking record company books
summary: Royalties from Basie material and air shots were once as high as $1,700 a check, then fell as ASCAP paid new rock and roll writers; auditing record company books is hopeless.

story.theme_name: Getting paid for records: royalties, publishing and flat fees
story.community_name: Royalties, publishing and who owns the song

blocks.x: Well, were you arranging as well all this time?
I wasn't doing any writing then but was heavy. the was heavy (unintelligible). My checks sometime would be as high as $1700.
Well, what were you getting the money on then?
That was on the Basie stuff and credits -- no, Ascaps was just credits for the air shots.
Yes, I see, yes. Performances on the air, that's right.
Yeah.
Well, what sort of royalties did you get from the -- from records?

I never was paid too well, only bread (inaudible) paid pretty well. Like maybe a couple of thousand a year and Metro-Goldwyn-Meyer, he's got the -- Glen Miller (unintelligible) -- oh, I was doing around about 10,000 a year in royalties. that was good.
Well, I mean, the thing I never understand is when you get those lists of royalties on records
and things, there's not a way in the world you can check that.

Yeah, but you see, they go down. They've been going down and I went to Ascaps and say, "Well, I got more action than I ever had in my life. Why are my royalty so low?" My battles, you know? And they said, "Well, we put on 50 rock and roll writers and we want to encourage them and we had to pay them something and (unintelligible)," because when they send out letters (inaudible), 90 percent of the members don't go and vote, so it ends up falling in the hands of officials, turned it their way. Then next year, be a smaller percent. (Inaudible) get more.
Well, I've looked at those lists of --
You don't get it.
-- record companies here and abroad, you know, come to me, and I mean, I've said to them, I've said, "Well, I can't -- who can tell --"
There's no way to do it. The lawyers try and they don't get to it.
There's no way you could find out what you -- I mean, you could send him to examine the books of Decca Records or somebody like that --
They'd give you set of books number three, something like that.
(Laughter.)
Right.
Supposed to be number one book. You know, never know the difference. They (inaudible).
That's what I think.
They bring it to court.

But then if you look at them like, for the six months ended now, six months from now, and -- I mean, those figures jump about so much and I can't see what the reason for it is, because suddenly -- well, I know one thing, though. One of those rock and roll groups did record "Stormy Monday" and he and Billy Eckstine got a hell of a lot of money for that.
Oh, yeah?
Yeah, but it's nothing to do with their records. It was with -- you know, one of the rock groups did it. So that, anyway, this is what you were doing for quite a long time.
